Europe Home page Europe 0 0 Lithuania says it would pay the cost if US establishes military base © APA | Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius 06 October 2026 12:34 (UTC +04:00) Lithuania is ready to pay the cost to set up a permanent ​US military base if Washington should ‌agree to establish one there, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius said on Tuesday, Reuters reports. On Monday, US President Donald ​Trump said he would consider Lithuania's request ​for a permanent base: "They are friends ⁠of mine, they are great people, so ​we will certainly look at it." Lithuania, a ​member of the EU and NATO, borders Russia and Moscow's close ally Belarus. The United States has ​kept an armoured battalion of almost ​1,000 troops there since 2019, in overlapping rotations, meaning ‌the ⁠troops arrive and leave every few months. Sinkevicius said he proposed turning this into a permanent presence at a meeting with Trump's ​envoy John ​Coale last ⁠month in Vilnius. "I'm glad that this idea is being taken seriously... ​This is a critically important ​guarantee ⁠of deterrence and security," Sinkevicius wrote on Facebook. "Our partners only need to make the political ⁠decision ​to permanently station troops, ​and Lithuania is ready to cover the costs involved." (EPA Images pic) WARSAW: Poland's prime minister Donald Tusk on Monday said that all Western countries should be more decisive in containing Russia, as the invasion of Ukraine enters a fifth winter. "This is the moment when the entire West – Europe, the US – should show Russia and (President Vladimir) Putin that it is ready to pursue a policy of containing Russia by even more decisive means," he told the Warsaw Security Forum, adding he was primarily referring to sanctions. "That is why I will go to Brussels to persuade all our European partners to seriously consider increasing sanctions against Russia," he added, ahead of a summit planned later this week. Poland – a Nato and EU member bordering Russia – has been a close ally to Ukraine since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, delivering critical military and humanitarian aid. It has repeatedly accused Russia of sabotage and hybrid warfare on Polish soil, accusations rejected by Moscow. In September, Tusk warned that Russia's plans in the war against Ukraine include "hybrid" drone and missile strikes against Kyiv's allies, including Warsaw. The centrist, pro-European prime minister has repeatedly maintained that Poland will remain a staunch ally to Ukraine, and he urged solidarity from other Western countries. His message came after US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire between the two warring countries without providing details, sparking astonishment in Kyiv and silence from Moscow. "If Ukraine fights, it fights for survival," Tusk told the Warsaw Security Forum, adding that "Russia fights for domination". "We in Poland remember very well how Nazi propaganda tried to convince Europe and the world that Poland was responsible for German aggression," he said. He emphasised that "today we hear exactly the same thing in Moscow, and unfortunately, increasingly often in some of our capitals".
